ego.name: Antoni Gaudí
ego.summary: Antoni Gaudí was a Catalan architect and designer whose highly individual work united structural experimentation, artisanal craft, natural forms, and Catholic imagery. Based mainly in Barcelona, he created works including the Sagrada Família, Park Güell, Casa Batlló, and Casa Milà, becoming the leading figure of Catalan Modernisme.

connections.relationship_description: Gaudí’s father was a coppersmith. Gaudí lived with him at Park Güell until Francesc died in 1906.
connections.notes: Gaudí was the youngest of Francesc Gaudí i Serra's five children.

connections.relationship_description: Gaudí's mother raised him in the family coppersmith household in Baix Camp and died in 1876 while he was studying architecture in Barcelona.
Gaudí lived with his niece Rosa Egea Gaudí in his house at Park Güell from 1906 until her death in 1912.
connections.notes: Her death was one of several losses that preceded Gaudí's final concentration on the Sagrada Família.

connections.relationship_description: Berenguer, the son of Gaudí's nursery-school teacher, became one of Gaudí's principal assistants and built the Park Güell house where Gaudí lived from 1906.
connections.notes: Berenguer's death in 1914 was a major personal and professional loss for Gaudí.

connections.relationship_description: Gaudí worked in Martorell's office as a student, and Martorell later recommended him to lead the Sagrada Família project after declining the post himself in 1883.
connections.notes: Martorell also connected Gaudí with important future patrons, including the Marquess of Comillas.

connections.relationship_description: Jujol worked closely with Gaudí on Casa Batlló, Casa Milà, and Park Güell, contributing decoration, color, ceramics, and related design work.
connections.notes: Their first project together was Casa Batlló.

connections.relationship_description: Rubió was a devoted disciple of Gaudí and collaborated with him until 1905 on the Sagrada Família, Park Güell, Casa Batlló, Casa Calvet, Bellesguard, and other projects.
Sugrañes became a trusted collaborator after meeting Gaudí in 1905, worked intensively on later projects, and directed construction at the Sagrada Família after Gaudí's death.
connections.notes: Gaudí named Sugrañes as executor of his will.

connections.relationship_description: Güell met Gaudí after seeing his work at the 1878 Paris World’s Fair and became his friend and patron. He commissioned Palau Güell, Park Güell, Colònia Güell, and other projects.
connections.notes: Their shared Catholic commitments reinforced a relationship that shaped Gaudí's career from its beginning.

connections.relationship_description: Rosa was one of Gaudí's two siblings who survived into adulthood; her death in 1879 was among the early losses in his close family.
Gaudí's brother Francesc became a physician and died in 1876, shortly after graduating, during Gaudí's architectural studies.

connections.person_name: Francisco de Paula del Villar y Lozano
connections.relationship_description: Gaudí drew plans for Villar and worked under him on the Montserrat basilica apse. In 1883, Gaudí succeeded Villar on the Sagrada Família after Villar left the project.
connections.notes: Villar's original Sagrada Família scheme was Neo-Gothic, whereas Gaudí radically remade the design.

connections.relationship_description: Matamala was Gaudí's friend and sculptural collaborator on the Sagrada Família and Casa de los Botines; Gaudí also shared the news of his architectural qualification with him in 1878.
Gaudí became a friend of Güell's father-in-law, Antonio López, and designed El Capricho for him in Comillas.
connections.notes: Martorell helped Gaudí establish contacts with the Comillas circle.

connections.relationship_description: Vicens commissioned Gaudí's first major residential work, Casa Vicens, in Barcelona's Gràcia district in 1878.
connections.notes: Casa Vicens helped establish Gaudí's reputation beyond his earliest small projects.

connections.relationship_description: The textile manufacturer Calvet commissioned Casa Calvet, designed by Gaudí in 1898 and recognized by Barcelona as its best building of 1900.
Batlló hired Gaudí to remodel his Barcelona residence, Casa Batlló, from 1904 to 1906.
connections.notes: Gaudí and Josep Maria Jujol worked together on the transformation.

connections.relationship_description: As director of the Barcelona Higher School of Architecture, Rogent approved Gaudí’s qualification in 1878. He remarked that the school had graduated either a fool or a genius.
Torras i Bages was Gaudí’s friend and a leading figure in Catalan Catholic thought. He died in 1916 while Gaudí was working on the Sagrada Família.
connections.notes: Gaudí belonged to Catholic artistic and Catalan religious organizations whose outlook aligned with Torras's thought.

connections.relationship_description: The Benedictine monk taught a Gregorian chant course at Barcelona's Palau de la Música Catalana in 1916, which Gaudí attended during his final years.
connections.notes: This contact reflects Gaudí's late-life concentration on Catholic practice and the Sagrada Família.

category_summaries.summary: Gaudí grew up in his father’s coppersmith household in Baix Camp and retained close ties to his family. His mother and brother died in 1876, followed by his sister in 1879. He later lived with his father and niece at Park Güell until their deaths, then moved into the Sagrada Família workshop in 1925.

Gaudí gained practical experience while drawing for established Barcelona architects, including Joan Martorell and Francisco de Paula del Villar. His studio later brought assistants and younger architects into projects such as Park Güell, Casa Batlló, Casa Milà, and the Sagrada Família. Collaborators preserved knowledge of the Sagrada Família’s construction after his death.

Private patrons gave Gaudí opportunities to build ambitious work in Barcelona and beyond. Eusebi Güell supported projects that ranged from residences and pavilions to Park Güell and the unfinished Colònia Güell church. Other clients commissioned Casa Vicens, Casa Calvet, Casa Batlló, and Casa Milà.

Architectural study in Barcelona gave Gaudí the qualification needed to practice. In 1878, school director Elies Rogent approved his qualification despite uneven grades and remarked on the uncertainty of Gaudí’s talent.

Catholic relationships formed part of Gaudí’s later life. His friendship with Josep Torras i Bages connected him with Catalan Catholic thought, and he attended Gregori Maria Sunyol’s Gregorian chant course in 1916. From 1915, Gaudí devoted his work to the Sagrada Família.
